title: The Logging Trucks That Filled Up
text:
In the early 1970s Gary Latham, then working with a forest products company, studied the crews who drove logs from the woods to the mill. Each truck could legally carry a certain weight, but drivers usually loaded only about 60 percent of what was allowed, so the company was paying for many more trips than it needed.

The drivers were simply told to "do your best." Latham and James Baldes replaced that with a specific, hard goal: load each truck to 94 percent of the legal limit. There was no extra pay for reaching it, no punishment for missing it, and no threat to anyone's job. Drivers only received the target and could see how close they came.

Within a few months, average loads rose to above 90 percent of the legal maximum, and they stayed there for the rest of the study. Drivers began to compete informally with one another and to take pride in reaching the mark. The company estimated it saved a large sum it would otherwise have spent on additional trucks. The study became a classic example that goal setting works not only in the lab but in real jobs.
lesson: A clear target and visible progress can change performance even without new rewards. Before adding incentives, make sure people know exactly what good looks like.
source: Latham, G. P., and Baldes, J. J. (1975). The 'practical significance' of Locke's theory of goal setting. Journal of Applied Psychology, 60(1), 122-124.
